description_full: Cimpress plc provides various mass customization of printing and related products in North America, Europe, and internationally. It operates through five segments: Vista, PrintBrothers, The Print Group, National Pen, and All Other Businesses. The company offers printed and digital marketing products; canvas-print wall décor products, business signage, and other large-format printed products; business cards; and marketing materials, such as flyers and postcards, digital and marketing services, decorated apparel, packaging, design services, textiles, and magazines and catalogs. It also manufactures and markets custom writing instruments and promotional products, apparel, and gifts; and provides professional desktop publishing skill sets for local printers, print resellers, graphic artists, advertising agencies, and other customers. In addition, the company offers graphic design, do-it-yourself design, website, and corporate solutions under the VistaPrint, VistaCreate, 99designs by Vista, Vista Corporate Solutions, and Vista x Wix brand names; and online printing solutions. Further, the company provides logo apparel, books, wall decors, photo merchandises, invitations and announcements, and others; website design and hosting, digital services, and email marketing services, as well as order referral and other third-party offerings. It serves various businesses, graphic designers, resellers, and printers, as well as teams, associations, groups, consumers, and families. Cimpress plc was founded in 1994 and is based in Dundalk, Ireland.

financial_summary: Cimpress PLC is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.4B market cap on $3.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 7% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $183M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.96× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 16% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 17% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 36% over the last three months.

On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 17.0 vs 23.1, EV/EBITDA 10.2 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 7.7 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 72% below its 10-year median.

prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 7.5%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.69).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.

hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($248.9M of cash against $1.6B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.3x.
The current ratio of 0.73 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
It runs on negative working capital (-29 days), so customers and suppliers effectively fund its operations.
Goodwill makes up 39% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.7% over 3 years and 7.6% over 5 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 22%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -4.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (2.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 24.8% on average.
own: Insiders own 16.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 91%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (13 sales, net $5.9M sold).
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (3.6% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 1.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 11.9% of the float, 6.2 days to cover.
people: With about 16,000 employees, each generates about $234K of revenue, 0.6x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 10.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $11K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
